w: Dr. Abou-Arraj split this session in two. He recorded the first part (posted Nov 9): the periodontal phenotype, recession and how it is grafted, the lack of keratinized gingiva and the frenum. "The remaining two mucogingival deformities," gingival excess and abnormal color, he covers "when we meet live this week." Until a capture of that class is posted, those sections come from his 2026 slides and the class exam-review guide, and they say so. The tissues: gingiva, alveolar mucosa and the MGJ The mucogingival junction (MGJ) separates the gingiva from the alveolar mucosa. You can often see it, but it is found "most accurately" clinically, with a probe. All the gingiva coronal to the MGJ is keratinized gingiva. Part of it is attached, to the root surface and the bone; the rest is free gingiva, the part a probe slips under to measure the probing depth. The line between free and attached gingiva isn't visible clinically. Mucogingival deformities Periodontal plastic therapy treats mucogingival deformities: "any deviation from the norm" in the volume, dimension, contour or shape of the soft tissue around teeth. The 2017 World Workshop classification (Journal of Periodontology, 2018) lists seven, and the slides walk through them in order: (1) the periodontal phenotype (thin scalloped, thick scalloped, thick flat); (2) gingival or soft tissue recession, described by surface (facial or lingual, interproximal or papillary), severity (Cairo RT1, 2, 3), gingival thickness and width, any NCCL or cervical caries, the patient's esthetic concern and hypersensitivity; (3) lack of keratinized gingiva; (4) decreased vestibular depth; (5) aberrant frenum or muscle position; (6) gingival excess (pseudopocket, inconsistent gingival margin, excessive gingival display, gingival enlargement); and (7) abnormal color (a mucogingival tattoo). The periodontal phenotype The phenotype has two parts: the tissue's thickness, thin or thick, and the gingival line's contour, scalloped or flat. Thin tissue can be judged by eye (you can almost see the roots through it), but the validated way is the probe: slide it into the sulcus. If you can see the probe through the tissue, the phenotype is thin, 1 mm or less. If you can't see it, the phenotype is thick, more than 1 mm. Why it matters: a thin phenotype is predisposed to recession, and recession that is already there tends to progress on it, while a thick phenotype resists it. His example: a young patient about to start orthodontics had a thin phenotype over his incisors, so thin you could see the roots. Orthodontic movement, then years of toothbrushing on top of it, would put him at risk of recession he didn't have yet. So before the orthodontics the phenotype was changed from thin to thick: a trapezoidal, full-thickness flap, a connective tissue graft from the palate sutured over the two central incisors (the teeth most at risk), and the flap put back over the graft to cover it completely. At two weeks the tissue was already thicker, and he was cleared for orthodontics with less risk of recession. Recession: what it is and who gets it Recession is "the location of the marginal periodontal tissues apical to the cemento-enamel junction" (AAP Glossary, 2001): part of the root is exposed. Measure it with the probe from the gingival margin to the CEJ, at the same six sites as probing depth, so it can be recorded and followed over time. It isn't only on the straight facial or lingual: note any interproximal recession too, because it "could change totally the prognosis of the treatment." It is common. The slide (Albandar and Kingman, 1999): 88% of people 65 and older and 50% of people 18 to 64 have at least one site with recession, and prevalence and extent rise significantly with age. In the recording he put it another way: more than half of the US population 30 or older has at least 1 mm of recession, and almost a quarter has at least one tooth surface with 3 mm or more. Older people have more not because of their age but because they have accumulated risk factors over more years. Recession is more common in men than in women and in African-Americans than in other groups, and most common on the buccal surfaces of maxillary molars (first molars in particular) and mandibular central incisors; canines are also commonly affected. Predisposing factors The slide lists ten: periodontal disease (periodontitis); trauma (toothbrushing, flossing, self-inflicted, foreign objects); anatomic variations (fenestration, dehiscence and abnormal tooth position); lack of keratinized gingiva; a thin gingival phenotype; orthodontic treatment; previous periodontal surgery; a high muscle attachment and aberrant frenum; iatrogenic factors related to the location of restoration margins; and the use of smokeless tobacco. What he added in the recording: Periodontitis, not gingivitis: attachment and bone loss expose the root. Previous periodontal surgery: after Phase I and resective Phase II therapy, "we caused most of this recession," on purpose, to leave an environment without pockets that the patient can keep clean. Toothbrushing is the most common traumatic factor: hard bristles, or an aggressive brusher whatever the bristle. The trauma list also takes in flossing habits, self-inflicted oral habits, foreign objects (a fingernail, a pen) and caustic medicaments applied directly to the gingiva. Anatomic variations. A fenestration is a window in the bone over the root; a dehiscence is missing facial bone from the crest apically. A tooth positioned buccally on the arch has thinner facial tissue and takes more of the toothbrush. Moving it back onto the arch orthodontically, into its alveolar housing, can resolve some of the recession, at least partly, without a graft. Put a dehiscence or fenestration together with a thin phenotype and an aggressive brusher, and you have "the perfect storm." Orthodontic treatment: pushing teeth buccally out of the alveolar housing (proclining incisors) over a thin phenotype can cause recession. Some studies find incisor proclination doesn't; he calls it controversial and advises caution about when to propose grafting. Iatrogenic margins: an intrasulcular or subgingival crown margin on a thin phenotype, an ill-fitting margin or an overcontoured restoration can lead to recession (which doesn't mean every crown needs a graft). A high frenum or muscle attachment pulls on the margin with every movement. Smokeless tobacco, held in one spot, usually the lower premolar or molar area, changes the tissue locally and can cause a severe localized recession. His worst case had no pockets and no interproximal bone loss, but recessions reaching the bottom of the vestibule, hard to treat even with several attempts. How recession develops Two mechanisms (from Zucchelli's textbook). Toothbrushing trauma, especially on thin tissue: the epithelium is abraded, the connective tissue under it responds with inflammation, an ulcer forms at the surface, and with continued trauma the margin recedes. Plaque-related: the same process as periodontitis (plaque in the sulcus with poor hygiene, apical and lateral migration of the junctional epithelium, loss of attachment), here on a local scale on a thin phenotype. "The key word here is inflammation": it is what actually causes recession, and the factors above are predisposing factors that make it happen. The Cairo classification: how much root can you cover? Before proposing a graft, assess how severe the recession is and what treatment can achieve. The Cairo classification (2011) has three types, read from the interproximal attachment: RT1: recession with no loss of interproximal attachment; the interproximal CEJ can't be detected clinically on the mesial or the distal. The best prognosis: about 100% root coverage is achievable. RT2: recession with loss of interproximal attachment, where the interproximal CAL (from the interproximal CEJ to the depth of the interproximal sulcus or pocket) is less than or equal to the buccal CAL (from the buccal CEJ to the depth of the buccal sulcus or pocket). You can see the CEJ interproximally. Expect partial root coverage, about 50 to 60% in cases like his: at best up to the level of the interproximal attachment on either side. The tissue can't be pulled any higher, because there is no framework and no blood supply interproximally to hold it there ("if we know how to fix this, we could ... cure everybody from periodontitis"). RT3: loss of interproximal attachment where the interproximal CAL is greater than the buccal CAL. A graft for root coverage "would not end up achieving that root coverage at all," so root coverage isn't encouraged. The classification is how you decide when to propose a soft tissue graft for root coverage, and when not to. Why treat recession Exposed roots and lost tissue raise the likelihood of (1) dentinal hypersensitivity, (2) soft tissue discomfort (thin tissue with little keratinized gingiva can hurt to brush), (3) root surface caries, (4) esthetic concerns, (5) interference with adequate mechanical plaque control, and (6) greater susceptibility to inflammatory insult. And recession doesn't sit still: a systematic review (Chambrone and Tatakis, 2016) found that untreated recession defects continue to progress, the margin moving further apical. So "let's just monitor it" because it doesn't hurt, isn't sensitive and isn't in the esthetic zone doesn't mean it will stay the same. Apart from RT3, recession should be considered for treatment when indicated. (Restorative ways to treat recession are for next year's course; this session is about soft tissue grafting.) Soft tissue grafts: where they come from The two main sources in the US are the patient's own tissue, an autograft, and donor tissue from a tissue bank, an allograft; there are others (bovine, porcine). The most common graft comes from the palate (or the tuberosity), because the palate is orthokeratinized: its tissue "carries that information of keratinization with it" to the recipient site. Palatal connective tissue induces epithelial differentiation and keratinization. From the palate you take either a free gingival graft (FGG), the epithelium together with the lamina propria (the connective tissue) under it in one piece, or a subepithelial connective tissue graft (SCTG, or CTG), the connective tissue without the epithelium. The palate's layers, from the surface in: the epithelium (0.3-0.6 mm, thin), the lamina propria (connective tissue, 1.25-3.0 mm, usually the thickest), the submucosa (adipose and glandular tissue), then bone. An epithelialized graft is thin at 0.5-0.8 mm, average at 0.9-1.4 mm and thick at 1.5-2.0 mm or more. A thick graft brings much of the fat layer with it, and that is usually removed so it doesn't slow the healing. The anatomy to stay away from is the greater palatine artery and nerve, the neurovascular bundle. On the slide it runs about 7 mm from the CEJ in a shallow palate, 12 mm in an average palate and 17 mm in a high palate. So a high, deep palatal vault gives the most room for error when harvesting (the exam-review guide's point). There are guidelines for which area to harvest from (premolar, molar) and how far up the palate to go. Two ways to harvest a CTG: a trap door, elevating the epithelium and connective tissue together and then taking the connective tissue from under the epithelium; or harvesting the whole rectangle with its epithelium, like an FGG, and removing the epithelium afterwards. The exam-review guide puts it this way: sometimes an FGG is harvested but delivered as a CTG, because that is easier to harvest and heal. The rule for which graft: if the graft will be covered by a flap, it must be connective tissue only. The inner side of the flap is connective tissue, and epithelium placed against it "just would not heal properly." If the graft will be left exposed, not covered by the flap, use an FGG, with its epithelium. Root coverage with a CTG and a coronally advanced flap His case: recession on #10 and #11 (part of a composite filling was removed first). A trapezoidal flap, raised partial thickness to keep some of the periosteum, exposed the roots; the graft size was planned (a template helps) and a CTG harvested from the palate, its epithelium removed. The graft was placed and sutured, then the flap was advanced coronally over it, tension free, so it holds its coronal position covering the recessions and the graft completely. At about four weeks the coverage was good, and coverage that looks like this early usually holds. The profile view shows the other gain: much thicker tissue over the roots, a thick phenotype "that by definition would resist much better" further recession. "We always do a coronally advanced flap if we're trying to cover the graft." Many teeth: the acellular dermal matrix allograft Treating many teeth from the palate means a large, invasive harvest. When you can avoid that, use a soft tissue allograft: donated human dermis, usually from cadavers, processed to remove the epidermis, the hair follicles and the existing cells. What is left, the acellular dermal matrix (ADM, or ADMA; AlloDerm is one), is a matrix of collagen, elastic and reticular fibers with no cells. It wasn't designed for dentistry: it has been used since 1995 for burns, head and neck reconstruction, urology (bladder slings, pelvic floor reconstruction), orthopedics (rotator cuff repair, periosteal replacement) and hernia repair, and in dentistry since 1997, now in dental sizes. It is the most common soft tissue allograft (exam-review guide). Advantages (slide): it eliminates the need for a donor site; increases patient acceptance (no surgery on the roof of the mouth); decreases surgical time; treats multiple defects in one procedure ("quote-unquote unlimited quantities"); achieves esthetic results comparable or superior to autogenous tissue; and is easy to use. Disadvantages (recording): it is "more or less a dead piece of skin" with nothing to contribute to the healing, "like a band-aid." So it must be fully covered by the flap, because it heals poorly left exposed without a blood supply. Over time it is remodeled and replaced by the patient's own tissue (histology shows this). In a more demanding site it can't give the same benefit as autogenous tissue; the exam-review guide's summary is that allografts don't work as well as autografts but have many advantages. His case: canine to canine, five or six teeth, with a combination of RT2 and RT3 recessions. The flap was a tunnel (pouch): like an envelope flap but without raising the papillae, going into the sulcus of each tooth and connecting sulcus to sulcus into one plane under the tissue. The ADM went through two water baths, the second with tetracycline, was snaked into the tunnel over the roots, held with sling sutures, and the flap was advanced coronally to cover it completely. At six months, given the RT2 and RT3 start, the result was considered quite successful. Lack of keratinized gingiva Keratinized gingiva (KG) runs from the gingival margin to the MGJ, and it can be thin or thick. Besides the color change (pink gingiva, redder mucosa), find the MGJ by rolling the probe, held horizontally, from the mucosa toward the margin: the loose, mobile mucosa rolls with it, and at the MGJ the tissue stops rolling. From there to the gingival margin is the width of keratinized gingiva. It can be measured on edentulous ridges too. On average (Lindhe's figure), the maxillary facial KG is widest at the incisors, narrowest at the canine and first premolar, and wider again toward the molars, and the mandible follows a similar pattern; on the mandibular lingual it is narrowest at the incisors and widens toward the molars. Patients vary. Is keratinized gingiva needed? A zone of attached gingiva is, of and by itself, not essential for keeping periodontal health and attachment, when dental plaque is controlled and there are no other traumatic factors (Kennedy and colleagues, 1985; Scheyer and colleagues, the AAP Regeneration Workshop, 2015). If plaque control is suboptimal, at least 2 mm of KG is needed to prevent attachment loss. Many patients don't have optimal plaque control, so a tooth with less than 2 mm of KG is likely prone to recession. That doesn't mean every such tooth needs a graft: it is case by case. Not every patient lacking KG has recession, but lacking it predisposes to it, while a thick phenotype with a wide band of KG resists it. Gaining keratinized gingiva: an FGG left exposed His patient had an RT2 recession on a sensitive tooth with no KG: the site was a plaque trap, chronically irritating the margin and leading to more recession. The goal was to change the quality of the tissue, creating a band of KG; root coverage would be a bonus. A CTG under a coronally advanced flap wouldn't do it: covering the graft with the only tissue there, alveolar mucosa, gains no keratinized gingiva, because mucosa doesn't become keratinized just because it covers a graft. So he used a free gingival graft with an apically positioned flap: a trapezoidal flap (a horizontal incision and two vertical ones) placed apically, and an FGG from the palate, with its epithelium, left exposed so it heals into a band of KG, bringing its own determination to keratinize. Covering it with the flap would deny it that. The palate heals by secondary intention. The graft is held only by sutures, so patients are told not to pull the lip down to look at it every day, to keep a soft diet and not to brush the area while it heals. At three months there was a good band of KG where there had been none, blending with the neighboring tissue (bigger on the apical side), and partial root coverage, as expected for RT2. Her sensitivity was gone, the site was easier to clean and less of a plaque trap, and the phenotype was thicker and more protective. The frenum and the vestibule A highly attached frenum can be a critical factor in the progression of recession: with the lip and every muscle movement in the area (not only when someone pulls the lip), it pulls on the gingival margin, which facilitates plaque accumulation and adds to the recession. In one patient, pulling the lip pulled all the way to the margin of a central incisor with no KG. In another, the frenum stood in the way of the esthetic result while her crowns were being redone (the provisionals had closed the black triangle), so a frenectomy was done before the final restorations. It is a quick, easy procedure: dissect around the frenum, excise the tissue that forms it in a diamond shape, and close the diamond with a few sutures that extend into the lip. The classification lists decreased vestibular depth beside it, and the slides show both together. Gingival excess (slides; the live session) The slides give four etiologies of gingival excess, each with its treatment. 1. Pseudopocket: gingivitis, the gingiva swollen coronally so the probing depth grows without attachment loss. Treatment: improved oral hygiene measures and scaling. 2. Gingival enlargement: gingival diseases modified by medications, phenytoin, calcium channel blockers and cyclosporine. Treatment: gingivectomy, improved oral hygiene and possibly a change of the contributing medication. 3. Inconsistent gingival margins: discrepant gingival margins of contralateral teeth, a gingival line discrepancy. Treatment: gingivectomy or an apically positioned flap. 4. Excessive gingival display, a "gummy smile." Treatment: gingivectomy or an apically positioned flap, but first find its cause, because it has several. Excessive gingival display: find the cause The possible etiologies, each with the finding that points to it on the slides: short clinical crowns (altered passive eruption), with abnormal tooth dimensions and proportions and gingival line asymmetries; vertical maxillary excess, with an increased lower facial third; a short upper lip, with a lip length under 20 mm; a hypermobile upper lip, with lip mobility over 8 mm; or a combination of these. Passive eruption and altered passive eruption In passive eruption the gingival complex migrates in the apical direction, gradually exposing the crown, until the dentogingival junction settles in a final stable position at the cervical level (Alpiste-Illueca). In altered passive eruption it doesn't, and the teeth look short: the clinical crown is shorter than the anatomical crown. Coslet's classification reads it on two axes. Type 1: a wider gingival dimension from the free gingival margin to the MGJ, with the MGJ apical to the alveolar crest. Type 2: a normal dimension, with the MGJ at the level of the CEJ. Subcategory A: more than 1 mm between the CEJ and the osseous crest. Subcategory B: the osseous crest in close proximity to the CEJ. Types 1A and 1B are the most frequently encountered. The treatment is crown lengthening, matched to the type: a gingivectomy only in Type 1A; an apically positioned flap in Type 2A; an apically positioned flap plus osseous surgery in Types 1B and 2B. The logic behind the rule: in a B type the bone itself sits too close to the CEJ, so the bone has to be moved, whatever the gingiva; in Type 2 the band of gingiva is only of normal width, so cutting gingiva away would cost keratinized gingiva, and the flap moves the band apically instead. Only Type 1A has both extra gingiva and room above the bone. Crown lengthening: the pretreatment evaluation Crown lengthening works on the difference between the clinical crown, what shows above the gingiva, and the anatomical crown, the enamel down to the CEJ. Before it, check the clinical parameters, probing depth, gingival health and the width of keratinized gingiva, and the radiographic parameters: the apical extent of any fracture or caries, root length and form, the level of the alveolar crest, and pulpal involvement (Abou-Arraj and Souccar, 2013). The esthetic evaluation His checklist on the slides. Facial symmetry: the facial thirds, and the facial midline against the dental midline; an increased lower facial third suggests vertical maxillary excess. Smile line (lip line): high, medium or low. Incisal line: it should be consonant with the lower lip. Upper lip, height and mobility: 20-22 mm for women, 22-24 mm for men, and normal lip mobility is 6-8 mm, measured with a caliper at rest and in a full smile. Gingival line: the central incisors and canines at the same level, and the lateral incisors 1 mm coronal to them. Tooth shape, dimensions and proportions: the golden proportion, which the slides show in nature, art and architecture. Seen from the front, the central incisor is about 1.618 times as wide as the lateral, and the lateral 1.618 times the visible part of the canine, so centrals, laterals and canines show at about 1.618 : 1 : 0.618 (the exam-review guide rounds it to 1.6, 1 and 0.6 for half the canine). On the slide a 9 mm central goes with a 5.56 mm lateral and 3.44 mm of canine. Treating excessive gingival display The slide's table: altered passive eruption, crown lengthening and restorative therapy; vertical maxillary excess, orthodontics and orthognathic surgery, and periodontics may be required to correct the gingival display; a hypermobile upper lip, lip repositioning surgery or Botox may reduce the display; a short upper lip, no good options. When several factors are present, a combination of therapies may be considered. Patient 1 A healthy 28-year-old woman: "I don't like the color of my front teeth" (generalized fluorosis). She declined orthodontics and wanted veneers. The esthetic evaluation: equal facial thirds; the dental midline slightly to the right; a high lip line at full smile; normal upper lip length and mobility; canted gingival and incisal lines, the incisal line not consonant with the lower lip; flat gingival heights of contour on #8, 9 and 10, with the margins of #7 and #10 more apical than those of #6, 8 and 9, a discrepancy across all the anterior teeth; and square teeth #8, 9 and 10 (the centrals 8 mm wide and 8.5-9 mm high, the laterals 6 mm wide and 7.5-8 mm high). With normal facial thirds and a normal lip, the gummy smile came from the teeth and gingiva, short clinical crowns and an uneven gingival line, so the plan was crown lengthening, then the veneers. The photos follow her from the planned gingival line on the cast, through the surgery, to the veneers, with healing at 1 week, 3 weeks, 6 months and 18 months. Abnormal color: the mucogingival tattoo The last deformity in the classification (slides; the live session): a gray discoloration of the gingiva or mucosa, a mucogingival tattoo. The slides show one case: the stained tissue over an anterior bridge was removed, a graft harvested from the palate was sutured in its place, and the area was recontoured with a gingivoplasty 3 months after the grafting.
